wave1.lens_self_description: Outside-view reference-class historian. I used only historical base rates: East Asian growth gaps after reaching roughly $25-28k PPP per head, Pritchett-Summers regression to the mean, the record of IMF China forecast errors, wind/solar/nuclear/LNG diffusion S-curves, and the record of solar forecast errors. The lens forbade episode-specific mechanism (China policy detail, Iran-war pass-through, module-price dynamics) and forbade looking up anyone's 2030/2035 forecasts. I ran no web searches. Every historical figure below is from memory, approximate, and should be treated as unverified.
wave1.q1_reasoning:
Reference classes, as the gap in the first decade after reaching the income threshold (country growth minus world growth, recalled values, unverified):
- Japan 1974-83: about +0.7pp (about 3.7% vs world about 3.0%).
- Korea 2001-10: about +0.6pp (about 4.5% vs about 3.9%).
- Taiwan 1996-2005: about +0.8pp (about 4.6% vs about 3.8%).
- Japan 1991-2000 is the bust case, at the wrong income level: about -1.9pp.
- The three on-class cases sit tightly at +0.6 to +0.8pp. Including Japan in the 1990s gives a fat left tail.

Pritchett-Summers: the best predictor of a fast grower's next-decade growth is the world mean plus a small fraction of its past excess. China's 2015-25 excess over the world was about +3pp. A decay of roughly 0.25-0.35 implies +0.8 to +1.0pp. Two adjustments:
- China's population is shrinking (about -0.2%/yr) while world population grows about +0.9%/yr. That costs about 1pp of headline gap relative to the analogs, which still had growing labour forces. This pulls the gap down.
- China is about 19% of PPP-weighted world GDP, so the world rate includes China and the gap is mechanically compressed by about 20%.

IMF forecast-error base rate for China:
- Before 2012 the 5-year-ahead errors were negative (the IMF forecast too low), by 1-3pp.
- After 2012 they have been small and slightly positive (forecast too high).
- The April 2032 WEO will carry NBS official prints. Official prints are smoothed and tend to land near targets, which cuts left-tail realisations and inflates China relative to independent estimates.

Mechanical anchor: the IMF path is about 4.5 / 4.0 / 3.7 / 3.5 / 3.3, a mean of about 3.8. The world path is about 3.0-3.1. That gives a gap of about 0.75pp. The smoothed-official-data adjustment adds about 0.15.

P50 0.9. P10 0.1 is the Japan-style balance-sheet or trade-shock case, partly muted by statistics. P90 1.7 is official data holding near 4.5-5%.
wave1.q2_reasoning:
Second-decade gaps for the same analogs (recalled, unverified):
- Korea 2011-20: about -0.4pp.
- Taiwan 2006-15: about -0.3pp.
- Japan 1984-93: about +0.6pp.
- Japan 2001-10: about -2.8pp.
- Median of the on-class cases is about 0pp. Ten to fifteen years after the threshold, the gap typically converges to zero or turns negative.

Pritchett-Summers: excess growth roughly halves again over the next decade. That takes +0.9 to about +0.4.

What moves China relative to the world:
- Working-age population falls faster in the 2030s (about -1%/yr), against world labour that is still growing. Negative.
- China is still further from the frontier relative to US income (about 30% of US per head, against Korea at about 50% in 2000). That leaves more catch-up room. Positive.
- Official-data smoothing persists. Positive, about +0.2.
- The China-in-world weight compression persists, at about 20%.

P50 0.3, P10 -0.7 (a Japan/Korea-style turn below the world), P90 1.2 (sustained frontier-tech TFP catch-up). The distribution is wide because the ex-ante dispersion of decade-ahead growth (Pritchett-Summers) is about ±1.5pp.
wave1.q3_reasoning:
Conversion: IRENA net additions ≈ 0.74 × IEA PVPS DC. I reason in IRENA units directly. A DC figure X converts to about 0.74X.

Anchor: IRENA 2025 is 511 GW. The steepest-growth phase was 2022-24, at +30-60%/yr.

Reference classes, measured 5-10 years after the steepest-growth phase:
- Global wind: steepest phase 2005-09 (+30-40%/yr), then roughly a decade of plateau at 35-65 GW with repeated dips, before the 2020 and 2023-24 jumps. Plateau.
- French nuclear: build peaked 1980-85, then collapsed to near zero. Decline.
- LNG liquefaction additions: lumpy waves with plateaus between them.
- EVs: still growing about 25%/yr 8 years after their steepest phase. Growth.
- Solar itself: after 2010-11 there were about 3 flat years (2011-13). After 2017 there were about 2 flat years (2018-19). Then growth resumed.
- Tally: roughly 50% of cases plateau or decline within 5-10 years, roughly 50% keep growing at about 5-10%/yr.

Forecast-error base rate: IEA and industry decade-ahead solar forecasts have been too LOW in roughly 90% of vintages since 2006, often by 2-5x. Two corrections temper this:
- Most of that error came from the cost-learning phase. The base is now 500 GW and module manufacturing (about 1 TW DC) is not the binding constraint.
- The near-term 2026 consensus already points down 8%.

Scenarios:
- Plateau (about 500 GW in 2026, flat to 2030): about 500-550 GW.
- Growth resumes at 7%/yr: about 650 GW.
- Strong growth (about 12%/yr, emerging markets plus storage): about 800 GW.

The forecast-error base rate shifts weight upward from a pure plateau-class median. P50 600 GW, about 2.7%/yr compound growth from 2025.
wave1.q4_reasoning:
Same reference classes, now 10-15 years after the steepest phase.

Wind's case: from the 2009 plateau level, 2019 was about 1.0-1.5x and 2024 about 3x. That was driven by a new market wave (China) after a long plateau. Mature-tech additions at 10+ years tend to rise slowly with the market, at about 2-5%/yr on average, with long flat stretches.

Net-basis caveat: IRENA counts net additions. Retirements of 2010-15 vintage PV, which is about 200 GW of cumulative stock, begin to bite around 2035 at a rate of perhaps 10-30 GW/yr. This lowers net additions slightly.

Forecast-error skew: a historical underestimate bias argues for a fat right tail. I set P90 1150 GW, about 2.25x 2025.

Left tail: the French-nuclear-style collapse is rare for a modular, cheap technology, but saturation of China's market (about 55-60% of world additions) could drive a decline. P10 400.

P50 690, which is about 1.15x my Q3 median.
wave1.q5_reasoning:
Base rate of at least one YoY fall of ≥5% in annual global additions, within a 9-year window during a fast technology's growth or maturation era (recalled, unverified):
- Global wind 2010-2024: at least 5 such dips (about 2010, 2013, 2016, 2017, 2021). In any 9-year window, the probability of at least one dip was about 100%.
- Solar 2009-2025: near-flat or down years around 2012-13 and 2018-19 on some bases. On the IRENA net basis, true ≥5% drops were rare or marginal (IRENA 2018 vs 2017 was roughly flat to slightly down). In 9-year windows that is roughly 50-70%.
- LNG and nuclear additions: lumpy, with frequent ≥5% drops in nearly every 9-year window.

Structural base-rate factors that make dips more likely in 2027-35:
- A single-country concentration of about 55-60%. Policy-cycle dips in a dominant market historically produced global dips: wind 2016-17 and 2021, solar 2018.
- Rising retirements on the net basis.
- The S-curve maturity phase, where volatility in the YoY change rises as growth slows.

Factor that makes dips less likely: geographic diversification of demand. The 5% threshold is small relative to historical policy-cycle swings of 10-20%. Raw probability 72.
wave1.q6_reasoning:
Regime weights:
- A (R ≥ 1.5): 15. EV-style continued growth at at least 8.5%/yr over 5 years. Solar's own record makes this less likely after the 2023-24 surge.
- B (1.1 ≤ R < 1.5): 35. Moderate market-tracking growth, as in mature wind outside surges.
- C (0.9 ≤ R < 1.1): 30. A wind-2010s-style plateau.
- D (R < 0.9): 20. China market saturation plus net-basis retirements, the French-nuclear-style tail, muted for a modular technology.

Consistency check against my Q3 and Q4:
- Ratio of medians: 690/600 = 1.15. That falls in B, near the B/C border, which matches B being the modal regime with C close behind. Mass in B or above is 50%, consistent with a median R of about 1.1-1.15.
- Ratio of P90s: 1150/870 = 1.32. Ratio of P10s: 400/420 = 0.95. Q4's distribution is wider than Q3's, which supports a 15% A tail and a 20% D tail.
- The implied median of R is about 1.1-1.15, inside B and near the C boundary. This matches the weights.
- Sum: 15 + 35 + 30 + 20 = 100.
key_drivers: The East Asian analogs (Japan 1974-83, Korea 2001-10, Taiwan 1996-2005) cluster at a +0.6 to +0.8pp gap in the first decade after the threshold and about 0pp in the second decade. Japan in the 1990s is the fat left tail.
Pritchett-Summers regression to the mean: China's excess growth of about 3pp decays by about 65-75% per decade.
China's labour force is shrinking (about -0.2%/yr population, about -1%/yr working-age in the 2030s) while world labour still grows. This headwind is larger than the analogs faced.
Mechanical compression: China is about 19% of PPP world GDP, which shrinks any China-world gap by about 20%.
The WEO actuals will be NBS official prints, which are smoothed and land near target. This biases the measured gap upward and thins the left tail relative to true growth.

S-curve base rate: about half of fast energy technologies plateau or decline in annual additions 5-10 years after their steepest phase (wind 2010s, French nuclear). The other half keep growing at about 5-10%/yr (EVs, solar after 2013 and after 2019).

Solar forecasts by the IEA and industry ran too low in about 90% of vintages, which argues for a fat right tail. This is tempered because the cost-learning surprise phase is largely over and the base is now 500 GW.
Concentration in one market (China about 55-60% of additions) plus rising net-basis retirements by 2035 raises the frequency of dips of 5% or more.

wave1.lens_self_description: Fermi Structural Decomposer: growth-accounting and bottom-up physical/demand arithmetic only. The lens ruled out historical base-rate reasoning and reading the simulation. I did no web search, so every baseline fact is the orchestrator's press-reported figure and I did not verify any of them.
wave1.q1_reasoning:
China 2026-30 growth accounting, in pp per year:
- Working-age population about -0.5%/yr, times labour share 0.5, gives -0.25. Participation and retirement-age drift add +0.05. Net labour -0.2.
- Human capital (attainment upgrading) +0.3.
- Capital: I/Y about 0.39 and K/Y about 3.4 give a gross accumulation rate of 11.5%. Less depreciation of 5.5%, K grows about 6.0%/yr, falling to about 5.0% by 2030 as returns fall; mean 5.5%. Times capital share 0.5, that is +2.75.
- TFP +0.9: frontier-catch-up residual in EVs, batteries, robotics and AI diffusion, net of misallocation and local-government-debt drag.
- Structural sum: 3.75. Official NBS reporting smooths toward targets (about 4.5-5 in 2026, drifting down), which I treat as a measurement-layer +0.3. China mean is about 4.05: path 4.6, 4.3, 4.0, 3.8, 3.6.

World ex-China, 81% of PPP weight. Each line is weight x growth = contribution in pp:
- India: 8.5% x 6.4 = 0.544
- US: 15% x 2.0 = 0.300
- Other advanced economies: 25% x 1.3 = 0.325
- Other EM and developing: 32.5% x 3.4 = 1.105
- Sum 2.274, so the ex-China rate is 2.81%.

World = 0.19 x 4.05 + 2.274 = 3.04.
Gap = 4.05 - 3.04 = 1.01, which equals 0.81 x (4.05 - 2.81).

What moves the gap: China-specific items only, namely property and debt deleveraging, the falling capital-return trend and the official-statistics floor. India's share rising slightly raises the ex-China rate by about 0.05. The Iran-war energy shock is roughly common to both sides.

Tails:
- P10 0.3: China averages about 3.3 (IMF-style 3.3 terminal arrives early, plus a property double-dip).
- P90 1.6: official prints hold about 4.6 on average.
wave1.q2_reasoning:
China 2031-35, in pp per year:
- Working-age population about -1.0%/yr as the 1960s cohorts exit, times 0.5, gives -0.5. Retirement-age reform adds +0.2. Net labour -0.3.
- Human capital +0.2.
- Capital: I/Y falls to about 0.35 and K/Y rises to about 3.8, so gross accumulation is 9.2%. Less 5.5% depreciation, K grows about 3.7%. Times 0.5, that is +1.85.
- TFP +0.8.
- Structural sum 2.55, plus the official-smoothing layer +0.3, gives a China mean of 2.85.

World ex-China, about 80% weight (China's share is about 20% once its share peaks). Weight x growth = contribution:
- India: 10% x 6.0 = 0.60
- US: 14% x 1.9 = 0.27
- Other advanced economies: 23% x 1.2 = 0.28
- Other EM: 33% x 3.3 = 1.09
- Sum 2.24, so the ex-China rate is 2.80%.

World = 0.20 x 2.85 + 2.24 = 2.81.
Gap = 2.85 - 2.81 = 0.04. Rounded up to 0.2 because AI and robotics TFP diffuse faster in China's manufacturing-heavy structure (+0.15).

Tails:
- P10 -0.7: Japan-style balance-sheet stall, China about 2.0.
- P90 1.0: China TFP about 1.5 with an automation offset to labour, China about 3.7.

At this horizon the gap is driven by China's own capital deepening and TFP minus India's weight gain. A common AI shock cancels to first order.
wave1.q3_reasoning:
Bottom-up for 2030, all in GWac on the IRENA basis. DC figures are converted at AC = 0.75 x DC, from the orchestrator's 511 / 690 = 0.74 ratio.

China: 250 GWac.
- Demand in 2030 is about 12,500 TWh growing about 5.5%, an increment of about 690 TWh/yr.
- Solar covers about 50% of the increment plus coal-share erosion, about 380 TWh. At 1,150 h, that is about 330 GW gross.
- I cut it to 250 for curtailment and price cannibalization under market-based pricing, with the provincial VRE share passing about 30%.
- Storage pack cost of about $60/kWh partially relieves this.
- Range 180-340.

Rest of world:

| Region | GWac | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| India | 55 | Needs about 50-60 GWac/yr for the 500 GW non-fossil target |
| US | 25 | Credit phase-out under OBBBA; about 33 GWdc |
| EU | 46 | About 61 GWdc, flat after the residential slump |
| Other OECD (Japan, Australia, Korea, UK) | 25 | |
| MENA plus Turkey | 35 | Saudi and UAE gigaprojects |
| Distributed Global South | 75 | See below |

The distributed Global South line breaks down as: Pakistan 10, Africa 15, SE Asia 20, Brazil 15, other LatAm 15. IRENA undercounts import-driven distributed solar, so I discounted it about 10%.

Totals:
- Sum: 250 + 55 + 25 + 46 + 25 + 35 + 75 = 511.
- Retirements of 2000s-2010s vintages are about -5.
- Rounded to a P50 of 520, about 2% above 2025's 511.

Module capacity above 1.2 TW/yr DC (about 900 GWac) never binds.

Tails:
- P10 400: China at 160 plus US/EU weakness.
- P90 700: China at 380 on storage-enabled absorption plus faster Global South growth.
wave1.q4_reasoning:
Bottom-up for 2035, all in GWac on the IRENA basis.

- Coal replacement adds about 100 TWh/yr.
- Solar share about 50%, so about 360 TWh. At 1,200 h with storage-shifted output, that is about 300 GW.
- Curtailment at a VRE share above 40% cuts it to 270.

Rest of world:

| Region | GWac | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| India | 70 | Demand about 2,500 TWh x 6% = +150 TWh, solar 60% = 90 TWh at 1,600 h = 56 GW, plus coal displacement |
| US | 35 | Data-centre load growth beats the absence of credits |
| EU | 45 | |
| Other OECD | 25 | |
| MENA | 50 | |
| Global South distributed | 115 | Africa 30, Pakistan 12, SE Asia 33, LatAm 40 |

Totals:
- Gross: 270 + 70 + 35 + 45 + 25 + 50 + 115 = 610.
- Retirements of about -15 (the 2008-2012 European and early Chinese vintages) are offset by about +15 of repowering upsizing.
- Net 610.

Tails:
- The wide P90 of 900 covers a scenario where storage below $50/kWh makes absorption non-binding outside China.
- The P10 of 420 covers China saturation with curtailment above 10% plus a trade-fragmentation shock.
wave1.q5_reasoning:
This is structural, not a base rate.
- China is about 49% of the IRENA-basis total.
- China's annual additions are policy-driven, with a year-to-year sigma of about 18%: deadline rushes in 2025 and 2026, then the mid-2025 pricing reform.
- A China drop of 10% or more with the rest of the world flat (+3%) gives a global change of about -3.4%. To clear -5%, China needs to fall about 15% or a US/EU policy cliff has to coincide.
- Per-transition probability of global ≤ -5%: about 8-10% while the trend is about +2 to +3%/yr. Over 9 transitions with positive autocorrelation, P is about 1 - 0.92^9 = 0.53, cut to about 0.45 for autocorrelation.
- Then +3 for the plateau-regime mass, which puts the trend near zero.
- Result: 48.

Risks named: a 2027 China post-reform second dip, US credit expiry at end-2027, and China curtailment caps around 2030-32.
wave1.q6_reasoning:
The point ratio is R = 610 / 520 = 1.17, inside B.

Consistency check:
- P(R < 1.1) = C + D = 43%, so the median R sits just above 1.1. That fits the point estimate of 1.17, because Q3 and Q4 errors are positively correlated (common China absorption and storage drivers), which narrows the R distribution relative to independent draws.
- A at 15%: needs Q4 of about 780 or more with Q3 at about 520, close to my Q4 P80. Or Q3 low (about 420) with Q4 above 630. About 15% is consistent.
- D at 16%: needs Q4 below 470 with Q3 at 520, about my Q4 P20 conditional on a China saturation path.
- Sum: 15 + 42 + 27 + 16 = 100.
key_drivers: China capital-stock growth falls from about 6% to about 3.7%/yr as I/Y declines from 0.39 to 0.35 and K/Y rises. This is the dominant term in the shrinking China-world gap.
China working-age population goes from -0.5%/yr (2026-30) to -1.0%/yr (2031-35), partially offset by retirement-age reform.
The official NBS smoothing layer, about +0.3pp vs structural, holds the Q1 gap near 1.0 against IMF projections of about 0.75.
India's PPP weight rises from 8.5% to 10% at about 6% growth, which lifts the ex-China world rate and compresses the gap.
China grid absorption (curtailment and cannibalization under market pricing) sets about half of global solar additions. Storage cost of about $50-60/kWh is the main release valve.
The IRENA AC basis (about 0.75x DC) and IRENA's undercount of import-driven distributed solar in Pakistan, Africa and SE Asia.
US tax-credit phase-out (OBBBA) and the EU residential slump put a ceiling on OECD growth. Module capacity above 1.2 TW/yr DC never binds.

wave1.lens_self_description: Outside-view reference-class historian. I used only historical base rates: catch-up growth gaps of Japan, Korea and Taiwan, Pritchett-Summers regression to the mean, IMF forecast-error history, and energy-technology diffusion and dip frequencies. The lens ruled out episode-specific mechanism stories and searching for other forecasters' 2030/2035 numbers. All historical series are from memory and were not web-verified in this run.
wave1.q1_reasoning:
Reference class: the growth gap vs the world in the decade after each economy reached about $25-28k (2021 PPP) per head. Gaps are approximate and from memory, PPP-weighted world.
- Japan 1974-83: about +0.8pp.
- Japan 1991-2000: about -2.0pp (balance-sheet recession, the analogue to property and debt).
- Korea 2001-10: about +0.5pp.
- Taiwan 1996-2005: about +0.9pp.
The class median is about +0.65pp, but the spread is wide and the left tail (Japan 1990) is fat.

Pritchett-Summers: growth regresses toward the world mean (about 2pp per-capita sigma). Their 2014 China projection (~3.9%) was too low against reported NBS data, a reminder that the published series tends to stay close to official targets.

IMF 5-year-ahead China error base rate: before 2012 it was biased low (actuals beat forecasts). Since about 2015 it has been roughly unbiased to slightly high. The 2024 Article IV path decays to ~3.3% by 2029.

The gap is front-loaded. The IMF's own path (4.5, 4.0, ~3.6, ~3.4, ~3.3) against a world rate of about 3.1-3.2 gives a 2026 gap of about +1.4 shrinking to about +0.1-0.2 by 2030, averaging about +0.6-0.7.

Headwinds vs denominator: China's working-age decline (-0.5 to -1%/yr) and property/LGFV deleveraging are the Japan-1990 pathway and drive the left tail. A world ex-China slowdown (end of the US AI capex cycle) that spares China's reported numbers raises the gap. India and EM growth (~6%) holds up the denominator.
- P50 +0.7.
- P10 -0.3: a Japan-style balance-sheet regime starting around 2027-28.
- P90 +1.5: reported growth holds near target ~4.5% while the world sags.
wave1.q2_reasoning:
Second-decade analogues (approximate):
- Japan 1984-93: about +0.4pp.
- Japan 2001-10: about -3pp.
- Korea 2011-20: about -0.7pp.
- Taiwan 2006-15: about -0.3pp.
The class median is about -0.5pp. In every analogue the gap narrowed or turned negative in the second decade.

Pritchett-Summers: by the 2030s, China's per-capita growth regresses to near the world mean. Its total-GDP gap then turns on demographics: working-age decline of about -1%/yr in the 2030s vs a world labour force still growing about +0.5%/yr, worth about -1.5pp to the gap on labour alone, partly offset by convergence TFP (China still at ~30-35% of US per-capita PPP income).

The world denominator in 2031-35 also slows (aging OECD, China itself ~17-18% of world weight), which cushions the gap.

Japan 1990 is the dominant left-tail analogue. Korea and Taiwan are the central analogues. I shade the median less negative than the class (-0.2 vs -0.5) because China's 2030s per-capita income is still lower relative to the frontier than Korea's or Taiwan's were.
wave1.q3_reasoning:
Everything is on the IRENA net AC-dominant basis, starting from 511 GW in 2025. Where I reason in DC, I convert with a 0.74 factor (IRENA/IEA PVPS 2025). For example, 800 GWdc becomes about 590 GW IRENA.

Diffusion reference classes, 5-10 years after the steepest growth phase:
- Wind (steep 2004-09): annual additions plateaued at 40-65 GW for about a decade (2010-19), with net growth only via the 2020 China rush.
- Solar itself plateaued 2011-13 and 2017-19 after steep phases.
- French nuclear: peak build 1980-87, then collapse.
- LNG liquefaction: waves (~2009-11 peak, trough, 2016-19 wave).
- EVs are still in their steep phase.

My rough base rate is about 50% plateau or decline, 35% moderate growth, 15% continued steep growth. The 2020-25 solar steep phase (about +25-30%/yr) and SolarPower Europe's ~-8% for 2026 fit the "plateau after steep phase" pattern. So 2026 is about 470 GW IRENA, and 2030 is centered about 15-25% above 2025.

Counterweight: IEA/industry decade-ahead solar forecasts have been too low in nearly every vintage since about 2006 (base rate of underestimation over 85%). This argues for right skew.
- P50 600 GW.
- P10 420 GW (wind-style plateau below the 2025 peak).
- P90 860 GW (about 11%/yr from 2025).
wave1.q4_reasoning:
Same IRENA AC basis, with DC converted at 0.74.

After about a decade of plateau, wind additions roughly doubled (2010-19 avg ~55 GW, then 2020-24 avg ~100 GW). The renewal came from new markets and the replacement and repowering cycle. Solar's 2035 fleet of about 6-8 TW implies replacement and repowering demand of about 50-100 GW/yr. That puts a soft floor under net additions, although IRENA net figures subtract decommissioning.

Mature-technology class: late-phase annual additions grow about 0-5%/yr. Over 2030-35 that gives 600 x 1.0-1.3. The underestimation base rate keeps a fat right tail; the P90 of 1150 implies sustained ~10%/yr after 2025.
- P50 720 GW (about +3.7%/yr from my 2030 P50).
- P10 430 GW (a prolonged China saturation plateau with no ROW offset).
wave1.q5_reasoning:
Base rate of at least 5% year-on-year dips in global annual additions during a technology's growth or maturing era:
- Wind (GWEC series from memory): dips in 2013 (-20%), 2016 (-14%), 2017 (~-4%, below threshold) and 2022 (~-17%). That is about 3-4 qualifying dips in 15 years, roughly 20-25%/yr.
- Solar: flat to negative in 2012 and 2018-19 depending on basis. Within 2008-2025 there were about 1-2 qualifying dips on the IRENA basis, roughly 8-12%/yr.

In the post-steep, China-dominated (~55-60% of adds) phase, policy lumpiness (tariff reform, provincial quotas, grid curtailment pauses) pushes the per-year hazard toward the wind rate. I use about 13-15%/yr.

Over 9 years, 1-(0.86)^9 is about 74%. A recovery rebound in 2027 after the 2026 dip slightly lowers the 2027 hazard. Hence 72.
wave1.q6_reasoning:
Implied ratio from my medians: R = 720/600 = 1.20, which falls in B.

The distribution of R uses the diffusion class:
- Continued steep growth over a 5-year window: about 15% (A).
- Moderate growth: about 35-40% (B).
- Plateau: about 30% (C; the wind 2010-19 and solar 2011-13 analogues).
- Decline: about 15-20% (D; the French nuclear analogue).

Consistency check:
- P(R < 1.1) = C + D = 46%. P(R >= 1.1) = 54%. So the median R is just above 1.1, consistent with a point ratio of 1.20 given that the Q3 and Q4 errors are positively correlated.
- The Q4 P10/Q3 P50 ratio (430/600 = 0.72) and the Q4 P90/Q3 P50 ratio (1150/600 = 1.9) bracket D and A, with about 15-17% tail mass each. Consistent.
- Sum: 16 + 38 + 29 + 17 = 100.

wave1.lens_self_description: Fermi structural decomposer: I worked the China/world gap out of growth accounting (labor, capital deepening, TFP, China at ~19% of world weight) and built solar bottom-up by region, with the DC to AC conversion stated. The lens ruled out historical base rates, reading the simulation, and web search; none of the orchestrator facts were independently verified.
wave1.q1_reasoning:
Identity: World = w*China + (1-w)*exChina, with w ~0.19 falling to 0.18. So Gap = (1-w)*(China - exChina) ~ 0.81*(China - exChina). This means 1pp of China-specific growth moves the gap by only ~0.81pp.

China 2026-30 growth accounting:
- Labor: working-age population -0.5%/yr, partly offset by later retirement (+0.1) and schooling quality (+0.3). Effective labor ~-0.1%/yr; at a 0.5 share that is ~-0.05pp.
- Capital: investment/GDP ~40% falling to 37%, K/Y ~3.5 rising, depreciation 5%. K growth ~0.39/3.6 - 0.05 ~ 5.8%/yr, falling to ~5%. At a 0.45 share that is ~2.4pp.
- TFP: ~0.8-1.0pp, net of falling returns to property and local-government (LGFV) investment.
- Structural sum: ~3.3-3.5%.
- Official NBS prints, which feed the WEO, have been running ~0.5pp above IMF structural projections (2023-25 targets met). Headwind adjustments: 2026 energy-price shock -0.2pp in 2026 only; deflation and weak household demand; tariff and anti-overcapacity barriers -0.1 to -0.2pp/yr.
- Reported mean ~4.1% (path ~4.6, 4.3, 4.0, 3.9, 3.7).

World ex-China 2026-30, PPP weights within the ex-China aggregate:
- US 0.19 x 2.0 (AI capex cycle +0.2) = 0.38
- India 0.10 x 6.5 = 0.65
- Other emerging markets (ASEAN, MENA, Africa, LatAm, Russia) 0.42 x 3.3 = 1.39
- Advanced ex-US 0.29 x 1.2 = 0.35
- Total ~2.8-3.0%; I use 2.95. The implied world rate is 0.19*4.1 + 0.81*2.95 = 3.17, consistent with the IMF's ~3.1-3.3.

Gap = 0.81*(4.1 - 2.95) = 0.93.

Tails:
- Downside (P10 0.3): China slows to ~3.3% on a balance-sheet recession plus an export-barrier cascade, while India and the US hold up.
- Upside (P90 1.5): the official series stays near 4.7 while the energy shock and a burst AI capex boom slow the world ex-China.

wave1.q5_reasoning:
Decomposition:
- Nine annual transitions.
- China is ~45% of additions and policy-lumpy: tariff resets, 5-year-plan windows (2030/31 boundary), and grid-absorption pauses. A China swing of -12% alone produces ~-5% globally.
- My central path is a near-plateau (~+2-3%/yr for 2026-30, ~+3%/yr after), so year-on-year volatility of ~±8-10% (sd) makes a ≤-5% year fairly common: roughly 25-30% per year under a plateau and ~8% under a growth regime.
- Weighting by my regime odds (~45% plateau or decline, ~55% growth) and allowing serial correlation (a single dip regime), the effective count is ~4 independent draws.
- P(at least one) ~ 1 - (1 - 0.18)^4 ~ 0.55-0.6.
wave1.q6_reasoning:
Central ratio: R = Q4/Q3 = 650/570 = 1.14 at the median.

I treat ln R as normal with sd ~0.25 (Q3 and Q4 positively correlated, so the ratio spread is narrower than the levels):
- A: P(R ≥ 1.5) = P(z > ln(1.5/1.14)/0.25 = 1.10) ~ 14%.
- B: P(1.1 ≤ R < 1.5): z from -0.14 to 1.10, i.e. 0.864 - 0.444 = 42%.
- C: P(0.9 ≤ R < 1.1): z from -0.95 to -0.14, i.e. 0.444 - 0.171 = 27%.
- D: P(R < 0.9) ~ 17%.

Sum = 100.

Consistency with my Q3/Q4: the medians give R = 1.14, which falls in B, and B holds the modal mass. My Q5 = 58 is consistent with C + D = 44% plus dips inside the growth paths.

wave1.lens_self_description: Outside-view reference-class historian. I used only historical base rates: middle-income growth-gap episodes, the Pritchett-Summers regression to the mean, the record of IMF China forecast errors, energy-technology diffusion S-curves and their year-on-year dip frequencies, and the record of solar forecast bias. The lens forbade episode-specific mechanisms (China pricing reform details, trade-policy specifics, module-glut economics) as causal drivers, and it forbade looking up other forecasters' 2030/2035 numbers. I ran no web searches, so every historical figure below comes from recall and has not been checked against primary sources this session.
wave1.q1_reasoning: Reference class: large catch-up economies in the decade after reaching ~$25-28k (2021 PPP) per head. Gaps against world growth, all from recall and unverified: Japan 1973-83 ~+0.5 to +1.0pp; Japan 1990-2000 ~-1.9pp (debt and asset-bust branch); Korea 2000-10 ~+0.5pp; Taiwan 1995-2005 ~+1.0pp. That gives a class median of ~+0.5 to +0.8 and a fat left tail (the Japan-1990 branch, about 1 case in 4). Pritchett-Summers: growth rates regress hard to the world mean (persistence ~0.3 across decades), so any gap above ~+2pp is out-of-class. IMF base rate: since ~2012, 5-year-ahead China forecasts have mostly been too HIGH by ~0.3-0.8pp, but world forecasts have erred the same way, so the gap error is smaller and its sign is unclear. China's official prints have also tracked targets closely, which narrows the realized dispersion. Arithmetic anchor: China ~4.5/4.0/3.6/3.4/3.3 gives a mean of ~3.8, against a world mean of ~3.0, for a gap of ~+0.8. Note that because China is ~19% of the world PPP aggregate, the gap is mechanically compressed by about 0.19 x (China minus rest of world). Downside tail: the Japan-1990 branch (balance-sheet recession) pulls P10 to about zero.
wave1.q2_reasoning: This is the second decade past the income threshold. The same reference class shows gaps shrinking toward zero or turning negative: Japan 1983-93 was still about +1 and then went well negative; Korea 2010-20 ~-0.2 to +0.2; Taiwan 2005-15 ~+0.5. Pritchett-Summers at a horizon of 5-10 more years implies the gap keeps decaying toward the world mean. China's working-age population shrinks faster than any of those cases did at the same stage, but that is mechanism and is not used here. The class base rate alone gives a median gap of ~+0.3 and a wide spread (sd ~0.75pp), since the realized decade gaps for these economies ranged from -2 to +1.5. Because of the 19% PPP weight, the world aggregate partly absorbs any China slowdown, which narrows the spread slightly.
wave1.q3_reasoning: Everything is on IRENA's AC-dominant net basis, starting from 511 GW in 2025. Where I think in DC, I use IRENA ≈ 0.74 x IEA PVPS DC. The steepest-growth phase was 2022-2024 (IRENA ~+45-55%/yr, then +30%). Diffusion reference class, 5 years after the steepest phase: wind's annual additions plateaued for ~4-6 years (2010-2015 flat ~35-60 GW, with dips) before growing again. French nuclear peaked and then collapsed (policy-bounded). LNG builds came in waves with a plateau after each surge. China-led EVs kept growing. Base rate: in roughly 60% of cases, annual additions 5-10 years after peak growth either plateau or grow slowly (<10%/yr), and roughly 40% keep compounding. Solar has twice resumed growth after plateaus (2011-13 and 2017-19). Forecast-bias base rate: decade-ahead IEA solar forecasts have been too low in nearly every vintage since 2006, often by 2-5x. Industry central cases have been closer, but slightly too high in the year after a boom. Combined: start from 2026 at ~470 GW (an ~8% dip), then 5-8%/yr over 2027-30, for a P50 of ~640. P90 (the IEA-underestimate branch continues, ~15%/yr) ≈ 880. P10 (wind-2010s-style plateau with no recovery) ≈ 470.
wave1.q4_reasoning: The IRENA AC basis is unchanged (DC/AC conversion 0.74 where used). Ten years after the steepest phase, the reference class (wind, LNG, hydro waves, coal builds in China) is mostly a slow-growth plateau. Global wind additions roughly doubled over the decade from 2010 to 2020 despite flat stretches. Starting from the 2030 median of 640 and applying ~4%/yr gives ~780. Upside: solar has repeatedly beaten its S-curve projections, and the IEA's chronic downside bias argues for a fat right tail, about 1200 at P90 (~13%/yr). Downside: the share of new capacity in mature-penetration markets saturates and annual additions revert toward replacement plus modest growth, roughly 500 at P10.
wave1.q5_reasoning: There are 9 eligible year-on-year comparisons (2027 vs 2026 through 2035 vs 2034). Base rates during growth eras: solar posted a dip of ≥5% or a near-flat year about 2 times in ~15 years (2012, 2018/19), with a single-year frequency of ~10-13%. Global wind posted a dip of ≥5% in about 5 of 20 years (2010-2030 window: 2013, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2022), a frequency of ~20-25%. The class rate rises in the plateau phase (years 5-10 after the steepest growth), when policy and price cycles dominate. With a per-year probability of ~10-15% and some autocorrelation, P(at least one in 9) ≈ 1-(0.87)^9 ≈ 0.71. Given that the reference class points to a plateau phase, I put it at 72.
wave1.q6_reasoning: R = Q4/Q3. Median R = 780/640 ≈ 1.22, so the median sits in regime B. I model ln R as roughly normal with mean 0.20 and sd ~0.30 (Q3 and Q4 errors are positively correlated, so R is narrower than the marginal ranges imply). P(R≥1.5): z = (0.405-0.20)/0.30 = 0.68, so ~25% (A). P(R<0.9): z = (-0.105-0.20)/0.30 = -1.02, so ~15% (D). P(R<1.1): z = (0.095-0.20)/0.30 = -0.35, so ~36%, which makes C = 36-15 = 21. B = 100-25-21-15 = 39. Consistency check: Q3 P50 640 and Q4 P50 780 give R 1.22, inside B (the modal regime). The P90/P90 ratio is 1.36 and the P10/P10 ratio is 1.06, so the wings fall in B and C. A at 25% covers the IEA-underestimate history, and D at 15% covers the wind 2010s-style mid-decade dip. The total is 100.
key_drivers: Pritchett-Summers regression to the mean: decade growth persistence ~0.3 compresses China's gap against the world toward zero by the 2030s

China's ~19% PPP weight mechanically compresses the measured China-minus-world gap
IMF forecast errors on China have mostly been too high since ~2012, but are partly offset in the gap because world forecasts erred the same way
Diffusion S-curve base rate: ~60% of fast energy technologies plateau or slow-grow 5-10 years after their steepest phase (e.g. wind 2010-15)
Solar forecast-bias base rate: IEA decade-ahead forecasts were too low in nearly every vintage, which fattens the right tail
Year-on-year dip frequency of ≥5% in growth-era renewables: ~10-25% per year, rising in the plateau phase
IRENA AC/net basis ≈ 0.74 x IEA PVPS DC; 2025 anchor 511 GW

wave1.lens_self_description: Fermi structural decomposer working through solar supply and market dynamics. I built every number bottom-up from growth accounting and regional, physical build arithmetic. The lens forbade base-rate or historical-frequency anchoring, reading the simulation, and web verification; the orchestrator's baseline facts are used unverified as given.
wave1.q1_reasoning: China true growth accounting, 2026-30 average. Working-age (15-64) population falls about -0.6%/yr, times a labour share of 0.5, gives -0.3pp. Labour quality (schooling) adds +0.4%/yr x 0.5 = +0.2pp. For capital, investment is about 40% of GDP, K/Y about 3.8 and depreciation 6%, so K growth is about 0.40/3.8 - 0.06 = 4.5%. I allow 5.5% for the early years, times a capital share of 0.45, giving +2.5pp. TFP adds +0.9pp. The total is about 3.3% true. Published NBS figures, which the IMF database carries, run smoother and higher because of target-anchoring. My reported path is 2026 4.6, 2027 4.2, 2028 4.0, 2029 3.8, 2030 3.6, a mean of 4.0. For the world ex-China (81% of PPP weight), each entry is weight x growth: India 0.08x6.3 = 0.50, US 0.15x2.0 = 0.30, EU 0.14x1.2 = 0.17, Japan 0.035x0.6 = 0.02, other EM/DM 0.405x3.3 = 1.34. These sum to a contribution of 2.33, so ex-China growth is 2.33/0.81 = 2.88%. World = 2.33 + 0.19x4.0 = 3.09%. Gap = China - World = 0.81 x (China - exChina) = 0.81 x (4.0 - 2.88) = 0.91pp. An Iran-war or energy-price shock that hits both equally does not move the gap. What does move it: China's reported smoothness when ex-China has a recession widens the gap, which skews the upside. A China property and deflation spiral that pushes the reported mean to about 3.4% narrows it to about 0.4. P10 0.3 corresponds to China at 3.4 and ex-China at 3.0. P90 1.5 corresponds to China at 4.5 with an ex-China slump to 2.6.
wave1.q2_reasoning: China, 2031-35. Working-age population falls about -1.0%/yr x 0.5 = -0.5pp. Quality adds +0.2pp. Capital growth of about 4.0% x 0.45 = +1.8pp, because returns keep falling and the investment share declines toward 35%. TFP adds +0.8pp. True growth is about 2.3%; with reporting smoothing I use a mean of about 3.0% (the IMF 2024 Article IV is already at 3.3 by 2029). Ex-China: India's PPP weight rises to about 0.10 at 6.0% (0.60). US 0.145x1.9 = 0.28. EU 0.13x1.1 = 0.14. Japan 0.03x0.4 = 0.01. Others 0.395x3.2 = 1.26. The sum is 2.29 on a weight of 0.80, giving ex-China growth of 2.86%. Gap = 0.80 x (3.0 - 2.86) = 0.11pp. India's rising weight pushes ex-China growth up while China's demographic drag deepens, so the gap converges toward zero. The downside tail (China reported at about 2.2%) gives a gap of about -0.6. The upside (China stays near 3.7% reported) gives about +0.8.
wave1.q3_reasoning: Conversion: IRENA basis = 0.735 x IEA PVPS DC (511/695 in 2025). China enters IRENA on an NEA AC basis. The 2025 split in IRENA terms is China 315 and RoW 196. For 2026, China dips to about 250 under market-based pricing and RoW reaches about 215, a total of about 470, consistent with SolarPower Europe's -8%. China 2030 bottom-up: demand is about 11,500 TWh growing 5%/yr, an increment of about 575 TWh. Solar takes about 50%, or 290 TWh, plus coal displacement. At an AC capacity factor of about 13%, 1 GW yields 1.14 TWh. Curtailment and cannibalization at about 25% solar generation share brake the build. Result: China about 260 GWac, with a range of 200-350. RoW 2030 (GW, IRENA basis), driver in brackets: India 60 (500 GW non-fossil 2030 target), US 45 (credit phase-out vs datacentre load), EU 70, MENA 40 (Saudi/UAE gigaprojects), Pakistan/Africa/SE Asia distributed 50 (partly undercounted by IRENA), LatAm 25, other (Japan, Korea, Australia, Turkey) 35. RoW totals 325, roughly 11%/yr from 196. The global total is about 585 GW, equal to about 790 GWdc / 0.74. The module ceiling of about 1.2-1.5 TWdc, about 0.9-1.1 TW on IRENA basis, does not bind at P50. P10 460 = China 200 plus RoW 260. P90 760 = China 350 plus RoW 410.
wave1.q4_reasoning: China 2035: cumulative capacity is about 2,400 GWac by 2030. Demand is about 14,000 TWh growing 4%/yr, an increment of 560 TWh. The solar share of the increment is held at about 50% by curtailment, but sub-$60/kWh storage raises absorbable VRE. Repowering of 2011-15 vintages adds a few GW only. Result: China about 280 GWac, with a range of 180-400. RoW 2035 (GW): India 90, US 55, EU 70 (rooftop saturation offset by repowering), MENA 65, Africa/Pakistan/SE Asia 90 (the fastest-growing slice: cheap modules plus batteries against unreliable grids), LatAm 35, other 50. RoW totals 455, decelerating to about 7%/yr from 325. The global total is about 735 GW, equal to about 1,000 GWdc / 0.735. That approaches the current module capacity, but manufacturing would have expanded by then, so it is still not binding. P10 520 = China 180 plus RoW 340. P90 1000 = China 400 plus RoW 600, with storage cost collapse unlocking higher VRE shares everywhere.
wave1.q5_reasoning: Structural decomposition. China is about 45-50% of global IRENA additions over 2027-35 and is policy-lumpy, with a sd of about 12-15% year on year in additions. RoW growth slows from about 11%/yr toward about 6%/yr. Global yoy change = 0.5 x China change + 0.5 x RoW change, giving a mean of about +3-5%/yr and a sd of about 6.5%. The per-year probability of a drop of 5% or more is P(z < -1.3 to -1.5), about 8-10%. Lumpy candidates: a 2030 rush at the end of the 15th Five-Year Plan followed by a 2031 dip, and a curtailment crackdown when China's VRE share passes about 30%. Over 9 year-pairs with independent draws, 1 - 0.91^9 = 57%. Positive autocorrelation, since a dip lowers the base for the next year, reduces that to about 52%.
wave1.q6_reasoning: Central R = 735/585 = 1.26, which falls in B. I take ln R as about N(0.23, 0.22), with the sd drawn from partly correlated Q3 and Q4 uncertainty. P(R >= 1.5) uses z = (0.405 - 0.23)/0.22 = 0.80, giving 21%, set to A = 20. P(R < 0.9) uses z = (-0.105 - 0.23)/0.22 = -1.52, giving about 6%, set to D = 7. P(R < 1.1) uses z = (0.095 - 0.23)/0.22 = -0.61, giving 27%, so C = 27 - 6 = 21. B = 100 - 20 - 21 - 7 = 52. Consistency check: Q4 P50 / Q3 P50 = 1.26 falls in B, the modal regime, so the bins are consistent with my Q3 and Q4. Q4 P10 / Q3 P10 = 1.13 and Q4 P90 / Q3 P90 = 1.32 are both B, so mass in A and D arises only from anti-correlated draws, which keeps those tails modest.
key_drivers: China's reported GDP smoothness versus true growth accounting. NBS target-anchoring keeps the reported gap high through 2030.
China working-age decline (-0.6%/yr to -1.0%/yr) and a falling marginal return on capital (K growth 5.5% falling to 4%) shrink the China-world gap toward zero after 2030.
India's rising PPP weight (0.08 to 0.10) at about 6% lifts ex-China growth and narrows the 2031-35 gap.

China's solar build is set by the absorbable increment: demand growth (575 TWh/yr), curtailment and cannibalization at about 25-30% solar share, and the post-mid-2025 market-based pricing that compresses project returns.
RoW distributed and emerging-market demand (Pakistan, Africa, SE Asia, MENA), enabled by sub-$0.10/W modules and cheap LFP storage. This is the fastest-growing slice, but IRENA undercounts it.
Storage cost (cell under $50-60/kWh) is the main lever that raises each grid's VRE absorption ceiling and decides between regimes B and A.
Module manufacturing capacity above 1.2 TWdc does not bind on IRENA basis before about 2035. The glut keeps prices at cost floors.
US policy (credit phase-out after 2027, tariffs) against datacentre-driven load growth. US additions are flat at about 45-55 GW.

wave1.q1_reasoning: Reference class: the decade after reaching about $25-28k PPP per head, gap vs world growth. Japan 1974-83 was about 3.7% vs world about 3.0%, a gap of about +0.7. Japan 1991-2000 was about 1.2% vs about 3.3%, a gap of about -2.0, the debt and aging tail. Korea 2000-09 was about 4.5% vs about 3.8%, a gap of about +0.7. Taiwan 1995-2004 was about 4.8% vs about 3.7%, a gap of about +1.1. The class median is about +0.7 and the spread runs from -2 to +1.1. Pritchett-Summers: growth rates revert hard toward the world mean, which pulls the centre toward +0.5. On IMF 5-year-ahead China forecasts, the IMF under-predicted China before about 2011 and over-predicted after (reference class, not verified). However, NBS-reported outturns land close to official targets, so realised published numbers have a floor that compresses the downside: published Chinese growth seldom undershoots consensus by more than about 1pp a year outside COVID. The current IMF track (4.5, 4.0, about 3.6, 3.4, 3.3, mean about 3.8) set against a world at about 3.1 implies a gap of about +0.7, consistent with the class median. The Japan-1990 tail sets P10. What moves China relative to the world: China-specific deleveraging and its demographic drag (a rate gap that persists), against the reporting floor.
wave1.q2_reasoning: Reference class: the second decade after the income threshold. Korea 2010-19 was about 2.9% vs world about 3.3%, a gap of about -0.4. The class median is about 0 with a left skew. Pritchett-Summers implies the gap should have mostly mean-reverted by years 6-10. China's demographic decline is steeper than Korea's was at the same stage, which supports a slight left skew. The NBS reporting floor still trims the extreme left tail. P50 is 0.0, with a wide symmetric-to-left-skewed interval.
wave1.q3_reasoning: I worked on the IRENA basis directly, with no DC conversion. The one cross-check: about 0.74 x IEA PVPS DC, so 580 GWac is about 785 GWdc. Growth in IRENA additions is decelerating: 2022 about 190, 2023 346 (+80%), 2024 452 (+31%), 2025 511 (+13%), 2026 expected about 470 (-8%). This is the classic post-steepest-phase signature. Reference classes: wind peaked about 2010 (about 39 GW), dipped 2013 (more than 20% down), and stood about 1.6x the peak 5 years later. Solar's 2011 plateau was followed by about 2.5x in 5 years. Single-country boom-bust analogues of China's 2025 market reform are Spain 2008, Italy 2011 and Germany 2012, which saw 60-80% collapses. China is about 55-60% of the global total, but a global aggregate dampens national busts. IEA decade-ahead solar forecasts have been systematically and severely too low; nearly every WEO from 2010 to 2022 under-shot. That skews me upward. Path: 2026 about 470, then mean growth of about 5-6% a year on the mature-diffusion base rate, giving about 580 in 2030. P10 is a Germany-style multi-year China contraction, partially offset elsewhere. P90 reflects the IEA under-forecast base rate (growth resuming at more than 12% a year).
wave1.q4_reasoning: Same IRENA AC basis; 720 GWac is about 975 GWdc. Reference classes for years 5-10 after the steepest phase: wind kept compounding at about 7% a year with a lot of noise (about 39 GW in 2010 to about 117 GW in 2023-24). French nuclear plateaued and then collapsed to near zero once its build programme was complete; that is the D-tail analogue for a technology concentrated in one dominant market. EVs and LNG kept growing, though LNG was lumpy. The class median is continued growth at about 4-5% a year from 2030, giving about 720 (R about 1.24). The interval is wide and right-skewed because the history of solar forecasts shows persistent upside surprises, while the left tail is French nuclear-style saturation in the dominant market.

A mature-phase rate of about 15-20% a year over 9 years gives 1-0.83^9, about 0.81, before allowing for positive serial correlation, which lowers it to about 0.70-0.78. wave_audit.wave1_spread: Q1: 0.70 to 0.85 (tight; all three built on the IMF projection track). Q2: 0.0 to 0.45. Q3: 540 to 580, with the Historian's P90 at 820. Q4: 660 to 720. Q5: 55 to 76 (the widest disagreement: the Historian borrowed wind's dip rate, while Fermi and the Scout used a China-shock hazard of about 8-9%/yr). Q6 B: 40 to 48. The main hidden flaw was the Historian's 2026 base of about 470, a DC dip applied to an AC series.
wave_audit.what_wave2_changed: The Bayesian incorporated the Scout's NEA telemetry, which cut Q3 to 515 and Q4 to 640, and anchored Q5 at 70 with a volatility-based argument. The red-team named the DC/AC basis error behind the shallow-dip assumption, argued that a lower trough raises R (A 22), and moved Q1/Q2 up on the grounds that the database records realised target-tracking NBS prints, not projections (1.05/0.6).
wave_audit.unresolved: Whether China's storage valve reopens by 2028-30 or stays policy-gated. This dominates the Q4 level and the A/C split. Whether NBS target-tracking survives past 2030 and the doubling deadline (the width of Q2). The true per-year dip hazard in a China-dominated mature series (Q5 ranges 55-76 across panelists). Whether NEA AC figures map one-to-one into IRENA's China row is assumed, not verified.
wave_audit.biggest_update: Two corrections, both accepted as real red-team or Scout hits rather than contrarian posing. Solar: the 2030 base fell from 580 to 515 because the 2026 trough is about -25% on IRENA's AC basis, not -8%. China gap: the resolution source is realised NBS prints, which have beaten IMF medium-term paths by about 0.8pp. That moved the Q1 P50 from about 0.75 to 0.95 and Q2 from about 0.15 to 0.45.
